newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-John Hiatt doesn't get big-headed over his career.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-John Hiatt doesn't get big-headed over his career.

text.p: By his own admission, John Hiatt is not much of a joke-teller but when it comes to making albums he is the clown prince of Nashville singer-songwriters.

The cover of his newest album, "Little Head," features Hiatt's disembodied head emerging with a smirk from an open zipper. The title track is a saucy acknowledgment of the power of the male libido and the illustration reinforces the point for anyone who is still a bit confused.

Wry humour has been a constant in Hiatt's two-pronged career, both as the supplier of songs to the likes of Bonnie Raitt, Iggy Pop and Bob Dylan and as a critically acclaimed performer in his own right.

"Little Head" is his first album since "Walk On" (1995), which garnered two Grammy nominations for the title song single. Both were released by Capitol Records, the fifth label of a 23-year career that has produced 14 albums.

Hiatt, 44, said the title track was inspired by an ex-tour manager who used to say, "You know you're in trouble when the little head does the thinking." And, Hiatt notes, "Being the canine, bovine creatures that we are from time to time, it's inevitable. It will happen. The brain will shrink to fit."

In an interview with Reuters, he quickly added that it was "long ago and far away" that his "little head" last got him into trouble. He and his third wife, Nancy, live the rural life in Franklin, Tennessee, 30 minutes south of Nashville, with three children and assorted farm animals.
PROLIFIC SONGWRITER

Prolific as usual, Hiatt wrote the songs for his new album in two bursts. While on tour with his band, the Nashville Queens, he composed eight tunes, two of which ended up on "Little Head" -- "Runaway" and "Graduated." The rest of the album was cut in eight days in a Los Angeles studio.

"I don't understand that approach of people spending a year in the studio making a record. I'd go out of my mind. I just couldn't do it. But a lot of people do it that way and have big ole' hits. So what do I know?"

Indeed, if critical acclaim could be translated into commercial appeal, Hiatt would be the biggest rock star in the world. As it is, he has to be happy with a devoted core audience that will always come to see his theatre gigs.

"Walk On" dropped out of the top 200 after five weeks. He was so disappointed with sales of his previous studio album, grunge-influenced "Perfectly Good Guitar" (1993), that he bought out his contract with A&M, where he made five albums.
Hiatt is philosophical about standing on the edge of greatness for a frustratingly long time. "I'm a late bloomer," he said. "I don't want to have too much happening at once. It riles me."

His parallel career as a songwriter is very "happening." Raitt covered "Thing Called Love" on her multi-Grammy-winning album "Nick of Time." Other clients include Rosanne Cash ("Pink Bedroom") and Three Dog Night ("As I'm Sittin' Here").
'TIMING IS EVERYTHING'

In the next year or so, Hiatt hopes to release a double album with cover versions on one disc and his own versions on the other, including some he has never recorded in a studio such as "Angel Eyes," a hit for the Jeff Healey Band.
"Now that country's totally dead, I want to make a country record," he said wryly, adding, "Timing is everything!"
A country album would bring him back full circle to his first two albums, "Hangin' Around the Observatory" (1974) and "Overcoats" (1975).

He recorded those in Nashville after leaving a chaotic family existence in his Indianapolis hometown to become a contract songwriter. More albums on different labels followed, usually featuring a few sardonic rockers and pretty ballads.

While honing his craft as a witty performer, Hiatt developed a booze and cocaine habit. His first marriage lasted a month, his second ended when his wife hanged herself just before their daughter's first birthday.

Then he cleaned up his lifestyle, re-married and made two of the best albums of his career, "Bring the Family" (1987) and "Slow Turning" (1988), which took four days and one month, respectively, to record.
In 1997, the bad old days seem to belong to a different John Hiatt. The new one celebrates the simple pleasures of life in such songs as "Pirate Radio."

"The pure excitement of having this song that has these transforming qualities to it flying through the air, being picked up by your receiver, especially in the car -- there's just something so beautiful and American about that whole experience. I love that."
